StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement

Junwon Seo Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Sushant Veer Affiliation: NVIDIA Research    Ran Tian Affiliation: NVIDIA Research    Wenhao Ding Affiliation: NVIDIA Research    Apoorva Sharma Affiliation: NVIDIA Research    Karen Leung Affiliation: NVIDIA Research Affiliation: University of Washington    Edward Schmerling Affiliation: NVIDIA Research    Marco Pavone Affiliation: NVIDIA Research Affiliation: Stanford University    Andrea Bajcsy Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Video world models (WMs) have shown promise for policy evaluation and improvement by imagining realistic future observations conditioned on ego-robot actions. While WMs can model distributions over futures, policy evaluation and improvement typically rely on nominal imaginations, which can miss high-impact outcomes of robot actions unless prohibitively many samples are drawn. To enable robust policy evaluation and improvement over WM imaginations, we propose StressDream, which steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified at inference time by optimizing the initial noise of diffusion-based WMs. However, optimizing high-dimensional noise is challenging: the optimization must reason about nuanced, scene-dependent target events in generated videos while avoiding out-of-distribution (OOD) noise that yields implausible imaginations. We address this with two complementary objectives: a semantic objective with a Vision-Language Model that provides informative gradients by reasoning about the generated video, and a plausibility objective that prevents the optimized noise from drifting OOD. With state-of-the-art video world models for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, we show that StressDream effectively steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified by text at inference time, such as task failures, enabling robust policy evaluation and improvement by identifying actions whose plausible futures include undesirable outcomes.
\captionof

figure Overview of StressDream. (Top): The initial noise of diffusion-based WMs is optimized to steer imaginations toward a target event specified by an inference-time prompt. While nominal imaginations may miss high-impact outcomes of robot actions, such as spilling, StressDream uses VLM guidance to steer imaginations toward such outcomes while preventing the high-dimensional noise from drifting into OOD, where generations become implausible. (Bottom): StressDream imagines high-impact but plausible outcomes of robot actions, such as task failures or collisions, enabling robust policy evaluation and improvement. Video results are available at the project website: https://junwon.me/StressDream/.

Keywords: World Models, Inference-time Steering, Policy Learning and Evaluation

1 Introduction

Video world models (WMs), or learned simulators of physical environments, have attracted significant interest in robotics, promising policy evaluation and improvement with substantially less costly real-world interaction [1, 117, 78]. At their core, video WMs are generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching [52, 59, 73], learning distributions over future observations conditioned on ego robot actions, and thereby capturing the inherent uncertainty of physical interactions or behaviors of other agents [7, 17, 39, 61] (top, Fig. StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement). For example, in robotic manipulation, dropping an open bag from high above the table may or may not cause its contents to spill, leading to either task success or failure; in autonomous driving, the same ego-vehicle decision can elicit qualitatively different outcomes depending on the responses of surrounding agents, such as braking or maintaining speed.

Despite learning rich distributions over future outcomes, policy evaluation and improvement with WMs typically rely on nominal imaginations [17, 38, 42, 41], which can under-explore the diverse outcomes they are trained to model. Naively sampling imaginations from WMs can easily miss critical outcomes without drawing prohibitively many samples, making it ill-suited to the role of WMs: exploring plausible, high-impact outcomes of robot actions for policy evaluation and improvement [128, 91, 108, 99], where plausibility refers to outcomes supported by the learned WM distribution. For example, when a manipulator drops an open bag from high above the table, the WM’s distribution may include outcomes both with and without spilling; in contrast, when the bag is placed close to the table, spilling may be unlikely or absent from the outcome distribution (bottom, Fig. StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement). The ability to imagine plausible, high-impact outcomes can therefore allow the latter action to be preferred during policy evaluation, while the former is downweighted or suppressed during policy improvement. This motivates the central question of our work:

How can we efficiently steer video world models at inference time to imagine plausible, high-impact outcomes for policy evaluation and improvement?

Our key idea is to optimize the initial noise of a diffusion-based WM, steering generation toward high-impact events specified at inference time (e.g., spills or collisions), within the distribution of plausible outcomes. The challenge, however, is to guide this optimization in extremely high-dimensional noise spaces (e.g., 11M dims [38]): the optimization must reason about nuanced, scene-dependent target events from generated videos, while naive optimization can easily push the initial noise into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions [95, 106], producing implausible videos. To address this, we propose StressDream, which combines a semantic objective, using a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that reasons about what happens in the generated video to guide generation toward target events, with a plausibility objective that keeps the optimized noise within the in-distribution region. Together, StressDream provides dense gradient signals for searching the high-dimensional noise space, while preserving plausibility of generations, enabling video WMs to explore plausible, high-impact outcome distributions for robust policy evaluation and improvement.

Statement of Contributions. We propose StressDream, a novel inference-time steering method for diffusion-based video world models. Our algorithm optimizes the high-dimensional Gaussian initial noise to steer generations toward high-impact outcomes while preserving plausibility. Through experiments, we show: (i) in controlled settings with access to the true system dynamics, StressDream steers WM imaginations toward target task-failure events only when such outcomes are plausible; (ii) on state-of-the-art video world models for autonomous driving [38] and robotic manipulation [42], StressDream enables robust policy evaluation by detecting high-impact outcomes, such as task failures, with substantially higher recall (54%→94%54\%\rightarrow 94\%); and (iii) this robust evaluation improves policy by promoting robust actions that avoid potential failures, increasing the success rate of a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy [57] (39%→71%39\%\rightarrow 71\%).

2 Background: Action-conditioned Video World Models

Video World Models. An action-conditioned video world model fθf_{\theta}, parameterized by θ\theta, models distributions of future observations 𝐨:=ot:t+H\mathbf{o}:=o_{t:t+H}, where tt denotes the time and HH is the prediction horizon [42, 91, 108, 70, 65, 125]. Each observation o=[I1,⋯,In,q]∈𝒪o=[I^{1},\cdots,I^{n},q]\in\mathcal{O} consists of nn camera images IiI^{i} and proprioceptive state qq, such as the robot joint configuration. The prediction is conditioned on an observation history 𝐨hist:=ot−h:t\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}}:=o_{t-h:t} and a future ego-action sequence 𝐚:=at:t+H\mathbf{a}:=a_{t:t+H}:

𝐨∼fθ(⋅∣𝐨hist,𝐚),where𝐨:=ot:t+H,𝐨hist:=ot−h:t,𝐚:=at:t+H.\mathbf{o}\sim f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}),\qquad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{o}:=o_{t:t+H},\quad\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}}:=o_{t-h:t},\quad\mathbf{a}:=a_{t:t+H}. (1)

Diffusion Models as Video World Models. Recent video world models [38, 42, 125] often instantiate fθf_{\theta} as a diffusion model [52, 101], learning a transformation between the data distribution, 𝐱0:=𝐨∼pdata​(𝐨)\mathbf{x}^{0}:=\mathbf{o}\sim p^{\text{data}}(\mathbf{o}), and a tractable noise distribution, typically a standard Gaussian 𝐱T:=ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈D)\mathbf{x}^{T}:=\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{D}), where DD is a noise dimension, indexed by diffusion time τ∈{0,1,…,T}\tau\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}:

𝐱τ=ατ​𝐱+στ​ϵ,where𝐱0:=𝐨,𝐱T:=ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈D),\mathbf{x}^{\tau}=\alpha^{\tau}\,\mathbf{x}+\sigma^{\tau}\,\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{x}^{0}:=\mathbf{o},\quad\mathbf{x}^{T}:=\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{D}), (2)

where ατ\alpha^{\tau} is a decreasing function of τ\tau and στ\sigma^{\tau} is an increasing function. Generation proceeds in the reverse direction by iteratively mapping a noisier sample to one at a less noisy diffusion time :

dτ​(𝐱τ,𝐨hist,𝐚):=𝐱τ−1=ατ−1ατ​(𝐱τ−στ​gθτ​(𝐱τ,𝐨hist,𝐚))+στ−1​gθτ​(𝐱τ,𝐨hist,𝐚),d^{\tau}(\mathbf{x}^{\tau},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}):=\,\mathbf{x}^{\tau-1}=\frac{\alpha^{\tau-1}}{\alpha^{\tau}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau}-\sigma^{\tau}\,g^{\tau}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}\right)\right)+\sigma^{\tau-1}\,g^{\tau}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}\right), (3)

where gθτg^{\tau}_{\theta} is the noise predictor (see Appendix A). Starting from an initial Gaussian sample 𝐱T=ϵ\mathbf{x}^{T}=\bm{\epsilon}, repeated application of this reverse update produces the predicted future observations 𝐱0=𝐨\mathbf{x}^{0}=\mathbf{o}.

Initial Noise as a Control Variable. Following (3), which corresponds to the probability-flow ODE [103], for fixed conditioning inputs (𝐨hist,𝐚)(\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}), the imaginations are a deterministic function of the initial noise: 𝐨=fθ​(ϵ,𝐨hist,𝐚).\mathbf{o}=f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}). Thus, all stochasticity in generation is governed by the initial noise, implying that selecting the initial noise controls which video is generated from the WMs.

3 Setup: Policy Evaluation and Improvement with Video World Models

Policy Evaluation and Improvement with Video World Models. Given an action-conditioned video world model fθf_{\theta}, we aim to evaluate candidate action sequences by imagining their future outcomes, which can then be used for policy evaluation [91, 108, 70] and improvement [42, 41, 99]. The predicted futures 𝐨\mathbf{o} are evaluated by a test-time criterion function 𝒞test​(𝐨)∈ℝ\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}(\mathbf{o})\in\mathbb{R}, which measures whether plausible outcomes with high impact on policy evaluation and improvement occur in the generated videos. These evaluations can be used to improve policies by selecting actions that avoid such outcomes [130, 48], or by training a policy π⁡(𝐚∣𝐨hist)\pi(\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}}) using world-model imaginations [42, 41].

However, when multiple futures are possible under the same action sequence, robust policy [80, 5] should account for the distribution of outcomes that are plausible under the ego robot action:

where the inner optimization chooses a Gaussian noise to steer the WM generation toward a worst-case plausible future that maximizes the criterion, while the outer optimization selects a robust action sequence that keeps the criterion low across plausible futures, even under worst-case outcomes. Various methods can be used for the outer optimization: 𝓐\bm{\mathcal{A}} may be a discrete set in a sampling-based solver [130], or a continuous action space over which a policy is optimized [41]. However, solving the inner optimization is challenging, as it requires optimizing over a high-dimensional noise space.

Steering Imagination via Inference-time Noise Optimization. Since the initial noise acts as a control variable for the generation of WMs (Sec. 2), the goal of the inner optimization corresponds to steering the WM imagination toward a high-impact outcome that remains plausible under the learned model. However, because evaluating each noise requires an expensive denoising process, repeated random sampling is highly inefficient and likely to miss rare but plausible critical outcomes within a limited sampling budget. Instead, we leverage the gradient of a differentiable criterion function to steer generation more efficiently, optimizing the initial noise directly via gradient ascent:

ϵi+1=ϵi+η​∇ϵi[𝒞test​(𝐨i)],where𝐨i=fθ​(ϵi,𝐨hist,𝐚),\bm{\epsilon}_{i+1}=\bm{\epsilon}_{i}+\eta\,\nabla_{\bm{\epsilon}_{i}}\left[\,\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}\!\left(\mathbf{o}_{i}\right)\right],\quad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{o}_{i}=f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon}_{i},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}), (5)

where η\eta denotes a step size. Although this first-order gradient ascent requires a small number of iterative updates, each involving forward and backward passes through both the WM and the criterion function, the dense gradient signal makes it substantially more efficient than zeroth-order random sampling for discovering noises that induce plausible, high-impact video generations [106, 60, 34].

Challenge: High-Dimensional Noise Space. While gradient-based optimization in (5) can steer diffusion model generation at inference time [106, 34], applying it to video world models is challenging because their noise spaces are extremely high-dimensional, e.g., ≈1\approx 1M in driving [38] and ≈50\approx 50K in manipulation [42]. The optimization must guide generation toward meaningful, scene-dependent target events while preserving plausibility under the learned WM distribution. However, naive optimization can easily push the noise into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions of Gaussian noises, producing implausible videos (Fig. StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement), and the test-time criterion 𝒞test\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}} must be differentiable while reasoning about nuanced, task-relevant events that vary across scenes. Moreover, solving (5) is inefficient because exact gradients require backpropagating through the iterative denoising process.

4 StressDream: Steering High-Dimensional Video World Models

To address the challenges of steering video world models, we propose StressDream, which defines a differentiable optimization criterion by combining a semantic objective using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with a plausibility objective that prevents OOD noise: 𝒞test=𝒞sem+𝒞pla\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}=\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}}+\mathcal{C}^{\text{pla}}. The semantic objective uses inference-time text specifications of high-impact outcomes to reason about whether the target events occur in the generated video (Sec. 4.1). The plausibility objective preserves the statistical properties of the standard Gaussian noise prior, thereby maintaining the plausibility of WM generations (Sec. 4.2). Finally, we approximate the noise gradient to avoid full backpropagation through the iterative denoising process, enabling efficient optimization (Sec. 4.3).

4.1 Semantic Objective: Steering towards Target Events with VLM Gradients

Since video WMs operate across diverse scenes and tasks, the high-impact target events for steering may change with the policy context, requiring a semantic objective that can differentiably score whether scene-dependent target events occur in generated videos. We therefore leverage the general video-understanding capability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) as the semantic objective. Given an inference-time text prompt 𝒍\bm{l} describing the target high-impact outcome, the VLM measures how well the generated video 𝐨\mathbf{o} matches the prompt. For example, in robotic manipulation, one may specify “the coffee beans spill,” while in driving, one may specify “a collision occurs.”

To obtain a differentiable score, we use Qwen-VL [8] and prompt it to output a single token, yes or no, indicating whether 𝐨\mathbf{o} matches 𝒍\bm{l}. We then define 𝒞sem\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}} as the difference in log token probabilities:

𝒞sem​(𝐨,𝒍)=log⁡pVLM​(yes∣𝐨,𝒍)−log⁡pVLM​(no∣𝐨,𝒍).\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}}(\mathbf{o}\,;\,\bm{l})=\log p^{\text{VLM}}(\texttt{yes}\mid\mathbf{o},\bm{l})-\log p^{\text{VLM}}(\texttt{no}\mid\mathbf{o},\bm{l}). (6)

Using the VLM’s single-token probabilities makes the objective differentiable, providing rich gradient signals for optimizing high-dimensional noise that generates an inference-time target event.

4.2 Plausibility Objective: Keeping High-dimensional Noise in the Typical Set

Diffusion models are trained to generate samples from noise drawn from a Gaussian prior. When the noise leaves the typical set [25, 13, 83], where most training-time noise samples lie, the resulting out-of-distribution (OOD) noise can produce implausible videos that are unlikely under the WM distribution or have degraded visual quality. Importantly, in high dimensions, the typical set is not the same as the region of highest probability density: some noise vectors, such as the zero vector, may have high density but are extremely unlikely to be sampled from the Gaussian prior (See Appendix B.1 for more details). Since gradient-based noise optimization can perturb the noise away from this typical set [95, 106, 34, 96, 49], we employ a plausibility objective that encourages the noise to remain within the typical set of the Gaussian prior, with a combination of functions of the noise that capture key statistics of high-dimensional Gaussian noise: 𝒞pla​(ϵ)=λ1​𝒞norm​(ϵ)+λ2​𝒞iso​(ϵ)+λ3​𝒞spec​(ϵ)\mathcal{C}^{\text{pla}}(\bm{\epsilon})=\lambda_{1}\mathcal{C}^{\text{norm}}(\bm{\epsilon})+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{C}^{\text{iso}}(\bm{\epsilon})+\lambda_{3}\mathcal{C}^{\text{spec}}(\bm{\epsilon}).

Norm Concentration. First, since the squared norm of Gaussian noise follows a chi-square distribution, ‖ϵ‖22∼χD2\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{D}, it concentrates sharply around the noise dimension DD [95]. We therefore regularize deviations of the noise radius from the typical Gaussian shell: 𝒞norm​(ϵ):=−(‖ϵ‖2−D)2.\mathcal{C}^{\text{norm}}(\bm{\epsilon}):=-\left(\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}-\sqrt{D}\right)^{2}.

Isotropy. While norm concentration enforces typicality at a global scale, the optimized noise may still contain local correlations or structured coordinate patterns that are unlikely under an i.i.d. Gaussian prior [106]. To encourage coordinate-wise independence, we randomly permute the entries of ϵ\bm{\epsilon} and partition them into mm subvectors {ϵi}i=1m\{\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where ϵi∈ℝk\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} and D=m​kD=mk. Under the Gaussian prior, these subvectors should behave as i.i.d. samples from 𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈k)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{k}), and therefore their empirical second moment 𝚺^=1m​∑i=1mϵi​ϵi⊤\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\bm{\epsilon}_{i}^{\top} should be close to 𝐈k\mathbf{I}_{k}. We therefore penalize deviations from blockwise isotropy as 𝒞iso​(ϵ):=−1k​‖𝚺^−𝐈k‖F2\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{iso}}(\bm{\epsilon}):=-\frac{1}{k}\|\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}-\mathbf{I}_{k}\|_{F}^{2}, averaged over multiple random permutations.

Spectral Whiteness. Even when the noise remains typical in coordinate space, optimization can introduce frequency-domain artifacts [30]. Since Gaussian noise has a flat expected power spectrum [104, 112], we encourage the noise to remain spectrally white. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} denote a unitary 2D discrete Fourier transform applied over the spatial dimensions of each noise slice, and compute the power spectrum 𝐏=|ℱ⁡(ϵ)|2\mathbf{P}=|\mathcal{F}(\bm{\epsilon})|^{2}. We aggregate 𝐏\mathbf{P} into BB spatial-frequency bins to obtain bin-averaged powers {p^b}b=1B\{\widehat{p}_{b}\}_{b=1}^{B}. To preserve spectral flatness, we minimize the variance of these bin-averaged powers, 𝒞spec(ϵ):=−1B∑b=1B(p^b−p¯)2\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{spec}}(\bm{\epsilon}):=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}(\widehat{p}_{b}-\bar{p})^{2}, where p¯=1B​∑b′=1Bp^b′\bar{p}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b^{\prime}=1}^{B}\widehat{p}_{b^{\prime}} is the mean power across bins.

4.3 Approximating Noise Gradients for Efficient Steering

Noise optimization in (5) requires computing the gradient of the criterion with respect to the initial noise, ∇ϵ𝒞test(fθ(ϵ,𝐨hist,𝐚))=∇ϵ𝒞test(d1(⋯dT(ϵ,𝐨hist,𝐚))),\nabla_{\bm{\epsilon}}\,\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}\!\left(f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a})\right)=\nabla_{\bm{\epsilon}}\,\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}\!\left(d^{1}\!\big(\cdots d^{T}(\bm{\epsilon},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a})\big)\right), where dτ​(⋅)d^{\tau}(\cdot) denotes one denoising step in (3). Although diffusion models are differentiable in principle, backpropagating through the full iterative denoising process (e.g., 5050 steps [14]) can incur high memory cost and vanishing gradient [33, 3]. To make optimization efficient, we adopt a score-distillation [3] (Appendix B.4), which approximates the gradient with respect to the noise using the gradient at the generated sample:

∇ϵ𝒞test(𝐨)≈β∇𝐨𝒞test(𝐨),where𝐨=fθ(ϵ,𝐨hist,𝐚)=d1(⋯dT(ϵ,𝐨hist,𝐚)),\nabla_{\bm{\epsilon}}\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}\!\left(\mathbf{o}\right)\approx\beta\,\nabla_{\mathbf{o}}\mathcal{C}^{\text{test}}(\mathbf{o}),\quad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{o}=f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a})=d^{1}\!\big(\cdots d^{T}(\bm{\epsilon},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a})\big), (7)

where β\beta is a scalar coefficient. This approximation only requires backpropagation through the differentiable criterion function, avoiding full backpropagation through the iterative denoising process.

In sum, StressDream optimizes the initial noise as in (5), using a gradient that combines the gradient approximation, the semantic objective (VLM), and the plausibility objective (typical set):

5 Case Study: Steering Dubins Car Video World Model

We first study StressDream in controlled settings where the system dynamics and uncertainty are known. Since we know the true dynamics, this setup allows us to test whether WM steering can effectively identify high-impact futures (i.e., failures) only when they are possible under the system.

Naughty 3D Dubins Car. We consider an image-based setup of a discrete-time 3D Dubins car with state s=[px,py,θ]s=[p_{x},p_{y},\theta], continuous angular-velocity action at∈[−1.25, 1.25]​rad/sa_{t}\in[-1.25,\,1.25]\,\mathrm{rad/s}, fixed speed v=1​m/sv=1\,\mathrm{m/s}, and timestep Δ​t=0.05​s\Delta t=0.05\,\mathrm{s}. The naughty Dubins car introduces uncertainty by randomly flipping the sign of the control input: δt=−1\delta_{t}=-1 with probability p=0.2p=0.2, and δt=1\delta_{t}=1 otherwise:

st+1=st+Δ​t​[v​cos⁡(θt),v​sin⁡(θt),δt​at],δt∈{−1,1}.s_{t+1}=s_{t}+\Delta t\,[\,v\cos(\theta_{t}),\;v\sin(\theta_{t}),\;\delta_{t}a_{t}\,],\qquad\delta_{t}\in\{-1,1\}. (9)

Each state is rendered as a 3×128×1283\times 128\times 128 RGB image showing the environment and vehicle. In this setup, instead of the VLM-based 𝒞sem\mathcal{C}^{\text{sem}}, we use the safety score defined as 𝒞⁡(s)=px2+py2−0.252\mathcal{C}(s)=p_{x}^{2}+p_{y}^{2}-0.25^{2}, which induces a circular failure set of radius 0.25​m0.25\,\mathrm{m} centered at the origin: ℱ:={s∣𝒞⁡(s)≤0}.\mathcal{F}:=\{s\mid\mathcal{C}(s)\leq 0\}.

Video World Model. We train a WM on an offline dataset of 4,0004{,}000 random observation–action trajectories. We train a safety-score predictor to regress the ground-truth score from an image, and train a diffusion world model, fθ​(ot+1∣ϵ,ot,at)f_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid\epsilon,o_{t},a_{t}), to generate one-step future observation (H=1)(H=1) conditioned on the current observation and action. The resulting noise dimension is 10241024.

Experiment Setup. We aim to detect action sequences that have a possibility of entering the failure set using WM imaginations. We construct an evaluation dataset of 5,0005{,}000 random initial state and action sequences. For each trajectory, we compute the ground-truth minimum safety score achievable under the stochastic dynamics in (9), and label it as positive if the g.t. minimum score is below zero, indicating that the trajectory can enter the failure set. We then perform open-loop world-model rollouts using only the initial image o0o_{0} and the action sequence, and classify an imagined trajectory as a failure, i.e., positive, if its minimum predicted safety score along the rollout is below zero.

Baselines. StressDream steers imagination by minimizing the predicted safety-score for 1010 optimization steps. We compare against sampling without optimization: Nominal (NN=11), and Best-of-N (NN=1010). We ablate StressDream without 𝒞pla\mathcal{C}^{\text{pla}}, and compare against classifier guidance (CG) [26, 69], which applies gradients during denoising instead of optimizing the initial noise.

StressDream reliably detects failures only when they are plausible. Fig. 1 shows that StressDream accurately detects potential failures in WM imaginations, achieving a high true positive rate, i.e., correctly identifying trajectories that can fail, while maintaining a high true negative rate, i.e., not falsely classifying safe trajectories as failures. In contrast, StressDream without the plausibility objective in Sec. 4.2 yields a low true-negative rate, indicating implausible failures are imagined without the typical set constraint. CG similarly produces many false positives by directly modifying the denoising trajectory, generating implausible imaginations. Random sampling methods (Nominal, Best-of-N) generate plausible imaginations, but are less effective at identifying rare possible failures compared to StressDream, often missing them even with multiple samples.

6 Experiments: Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement

In this section, we validate StressDream for robust policy evaluation and improvement using state-of-the-art video world models in both autonomous driving [38] and robotic manipulation [42].

Autonomous Driving. We use Vista [38] that predicts 2525 future front-view camera frames at 576×1024576\times 1024, conditioned on future waypoints as actions, with noise dimension D=921,600D=921{,}600. We fine-tune the model on the PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles (PAI-AV) dataset [86] and the Nexar Collision Prediction Dataset [81], which include diverse driving scenarios such as collisions. We optimize for 2020 steps with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct [10] fine-tuned with Wolf [67] and X-CLIP [76].

Robotic Manipulation. We use Ctrl-World [42] trained in the DROID setup [62], which predicts 55 future frames from 33 camera views of resolution 192×320192\times 320, conditioned on joint-position actions, with D=57,600D=57{,}600. We consider six contact-rich manipulation tasks (See Fig. 6) and collect approximately 150150 teleoperation trajectories per task containing both successes and failures to fine-tune the model. We optimize noise for 1010 steps using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct [9], providing the three-view videos along with a prompt describing the task failure (More details in Appendix D.1).

6.1 Robust Policy Evaluation using State-of-the-Art Video World Models

We first study whether StressDream enables robust policy evaluation by efficiently steering WM imaginations toward high-impact but plausible outcomes specified at inference time. As a baseline, we compare against random generation (Best-of-N), which samples multiple imaginations without optimization with the same budget as StressDream, and selects the one with the highest score.

Evaluation Setup. We generate imaginations from an initial observation o0o_{0} and action sequence 𝐚\mathbf{a}, and evaluate whether the generated video matches the inference-time text specification 𝒍\bm{l} of the target event. For driving, we curate 100100 image–action–text pairs from the PAI-AV dataset [86] across 88 safety-critical event categories (see Appendix D.3), as well as 200200 imminent-collision examples [81]. Each prompt describes a target event that has not yet occurred in the initial observation but occurs within the prediction horizon. For manipulation, we collect 100100 failure trajectories across tasks as an evaluation dataset, and evaluate whether WM imaginations from the initial images and the action sequences can reliably identify failures (See Appendix D.2).

Evaluation Metrics. For driving, we report target alignment and video quality using a held-out evaluator, WorldModelBench [68]. Target alignment measures whether the video matches the text description of the target event, while video quality serves as a proxy for plausibility. For manipulation, we label each generation as a success or failure based on human judgment. (See Appendix D.4)

StressDream robustly detects high-impact outcomes in imaginations. Fig. 2 compares nominal and steered generations. StressDream plausibly generates videos aligned with inference-time specifications of target safety-critical or failure events that nominal imaginations miss, enabling robust evaluation of action sequences through WM imaginations. Fig. 3 shows that, without the typical-set constraint, both target-alignment and video-quality scores decrease, indicating that the plausibility objective helps preserve plausibility. For manipulation, StressDream detects task-failure events in imagination with higher recall, whereas random generations are often overly optimistic and miss possible failures, as shown in Fig. 4. More results in Appendix E.1 & Website.

Steering is grounded in plausible outcomes. We study whether steering remains grounded in plausible outcomes supported by the WM’s distribution, rather than hallucinating implausible futures. To test this, we steer generations toward collision events using both the collision-finetuned Vista model and the base Vista model, which is not trained on collision events. Fig. 5 shows that the base model cannot imagine collision outcomes even with steering, achieving lower target-alignment scores than random sampling from the collision-finetuned model. This indicates that StressDream steers only toward events supported by the WM outcome distribution, rather than synthesizing implausible events. Similarly, the right two columns of Fig. 2 show that target spilling outcomes are induced only when plausible under the WM distribution: StressDream does not induce spilling for the open sticky candy bag or closed coffee bag, but does so for the open coffee bag. Since sticky candies are unlikely to spill and a closed bag does not expose its contents, spilling is not supported by the WM distribution in those scenes. More details and results in Appendix E.3.

6.2 Policy Improvement with Steered Video World Model Imaginations

Setup. We study whether StressDream can improve a robotic policy through steered WM imaginations, promoting robust actions that remain successful over the distribution of outcomes. We consider improving a behavior-cloning policy, the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model π0.5\pi_{0.5} [57], with action evaluation in WM imaginations. Specifically, we fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5}-droid with 4040 successful demonstrations per task using a weighted regression objective [41], and compare two settings: Nominal π0.5FT\pi_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}}, which assigns a uniform weight of 1.01.0 to all trajectories, and Robust π0.5FT\pi_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}}, which assigns weight 1.01.0 to trajectories that remain successful under steering toward task failures and weight 0.10.1 to trajectories that fail in steered imaginations. This encourages robust actions whose plausible outcome distribution does not include failures, while downweighting risky actions that can fail.

StressDream improves policies by promoting robust actions. Fig. 6 illustrates rollouts of fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies. Robust π0.5FT\pi_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}} favors actions whose plausible outcomes do not include task failures, as identified by steering imaginations. In contrast, Nominal π0.5FT\pi_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}} proposes risky actions whose plausible outcome distribution includes failures, even if they happened to succeed during data collection. Fig. 7 reports success rates over 2020 rollouts per task, showing that Robust π0.5FT\pi_{0.5}^{\mathrm{FT}} achieves higher success by proposing robust actions that avoid potential failures.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we propose StressDream, which steers video world model imaginations toward high-impact outcomes specified at inference-time, while remaining within the distribution of plausible outcomes. StressDream optimizes the high-dimensional initial noise of diffusion-based video world models using a combination of semantic and plausibility objectives: VLM gradients steer generation toward high-impact outcomes specified by inference-time prompts, while typical-set constraints keep the high-dimensional noise typical under the Gaussian prior. With WMs for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, we demonstrate that StressDream effectively steers imaginations while preserving plausibility, enabling robust policy evaluation by identifying actions with potential failures and improving policies by favoring robust actions that avoid such failures.

Limitations. StressDream requires specifying high-impact outcomes with text descriptions, so its effectiveness depends on prompt quality and may suffer from reward hacking, where the score increases without meaningful changes in generations [34, 55], highlighting the need for generalizable and robust reward models for robotics [105, 71]. In addition, StressDream may fail to preserve plausibility or to discover relevant failures when the base WM is limited: it may steer within flawed videos produced by the WM, or fail to imagine target outcomes absent from the WM’s training distribution. Thus, our notion of plausibility is limited to what the WM supports, and does not necessarily imply physical plausibility in the real world, underscoring the need for diverse robot data to train high-fidelity WMs with physically consistent predictions. Runtime also remains expensive, as current WMs take several minutes per imagination [38, 42], though this could be reduced by efficient models [102, 64, 32]. We refer readers to Appendix F for a more detailed discussion.

Appendix

Appendix A Background

A.1 Related Works

World Models for Robotics. World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotics, enabling the prediction of future states directly from high-dimensional sensory observations conditioned on actions [36, 31, 44, 122, 130, 79, 15, 1, 77]. By generating synthetic trajectories, they have proven effective for vision-based policy learning [43, 45, 46, 47, 82, 2, 99, 41], planning in latent space [130, 90], and policy evaluation [48, 42, 91]. Advances in video generation models [14], which produce realistic and temporally consistent predictions, have further increased the expressiveness of world models in diverse real-world scenarios, especially when fine-tuned with embodiment data for action conditioning [38, 50, 42]. World models typically operate under partial observability, which naturally gives rise to uncertainty and multimodality in future predictions [114, 129, 61], particularly in settings such as contact-rich manipulation [42] or autonomous driving [38, 94, 11, 50]. In particular, diffusion- and flow-matching-based [52, 59, 73] approaches have shown strong performance in modeling high-dimensional, complex environments due to their ability to capture rich, multimodal distributions over future observations [7, 17, 39, 61]. Despite this, many existing methods using world models either rely on nominal rollouts without reasoning over distribution over plausible futures [17, 42, 98] or adopt deterministic world models that cannot represent such diversity [130, 77], thereby failing to explicitly account for risks arising from uncertain futures.

Inference-time Steering of Generative Models. Inference-time steering of diffusion [52, 103] or flow-matching [73, 74] model aims to guide a pretrained generative model toward samples that maximize an inference-time reward [106, 110, 111, 54]. While directly fine-tuning diffusion models with reward objectives can be effective for reward alignment [35, 115, 89, 24, 110, 28], it is costly, complex, tied to a specific reward [106, 54], and may shift the model away from the original data distribution [33]. In contrast, inference-time steering keeps the pretrained model fixed and instead modifies the sampling procedure [23, 51, 106, 111, 100, 126], for example through classifier guidance [103] or particle-based sampling methods such as Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) [121, 29, 88, 54]. One particularly relevant direction is noise optimization, which optimizes the noise sampled at the denoising process [116, 40, 60, 34, 85, 106]. Prior work has shown that this can improve image quality [40, 18, 33], mimic the effects of diffusion guidance [3], generate rare [95, 96, 97] or diverse concepts [63], and adapt diffusion policies in robotic control [113]. However, a central challenge, especially when the noise space becomes high-dimensional, is out-of-distribution noise: samples may achieve high reward while no longer remaining in the support of the pretrained distribution once the noise deviates from the prior [95, 12, 106, 34, 127, 33, 49]. Moreover, these methods often require backpropagating reward gradients through the denoising process; in practice, many therefore rely on step-distilled models to make backpropagation tractable [84, 34, 33, 27], while recent works propose multistep score distillation to approximate reward gradients to the initial noise more efficiently [3]. Our approach adopts initial noise optimization to steer action-conditioned video world models [38, 42] with a practical solution for high-dimensional noise optimization.

A.2 Diffusion Models

Recent generative models are often based on diffusion or flow-matching formulations, which generate samples from noise by simulating a learned differential equation. This section expands on the diffusion-model formulation in Sec. 3, which provides the foundation for recent video world models capable of generating high-quality videos. We omit conditioning on (𝐨hist,𝐚)(\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}) throughout for brevity.

Forward Probability Path. Score-based diffusion models [52, 59, 101] and flow-matching models [6, 73] define generative models fθf_{\theta} whose sampling process can be described by a stochastic or ordinary differential equation (SDE or ODE). The denoising network gθτg^{\tau}_{\theta}, which parameterizes these dynamics, is trained to recover the reverse generative process, typically by predicting the score of the perturbed data distribution, the injected noise, or the conditional vector field.

Starting from clean data 𝐱=𝐨∼pdata​(o)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{o}\sim p^{\text{data}}(o) and isotropic Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}), the forward process, indexed by diffusion time τ∈{0,1,…,T}\tau\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}, defines a perturbed sample as

𝐱τ=ατ​𝐱+στ​ϵ.\mathbf{x}^{\tau}=\alpha^{\tau}\,\mathbf{x}+\sigma^{\tau}\,\bm{\epsilon}. (10)

For variance-preserving parameterizations such as DDPM, the boundary conditions satisfy α0=1\alpha^{0}=1, σ0=0\sigma^{0}=0, and αT→0\alpha^{T}\to 0, σT→1\sigma^{T}\to 1. More generally, we only require that the terminal state be noise-dominated. Representative examples include the variance-preserving schedule of DDPM [52], where (ατ)2+(στ)2=1(\alpha^{\tau})^{2}+(\sigma^{\tau})^{2}=1, and the variance-exploding schedule of EDM [59], where ατ≡1\alpha^{\tau}\equiv 1 and στ\sigma^{\tau} increases with diffusion time.

Training Objective. The denoiser gθτg^{\tau}_{\theta} is trained to recover the injected Gaussian noise from a perturbed future observation, conditioned on the observation history and action sequence. With the noise-prediction parameterization,

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼𝐱∼pdata,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈),τ​[w⁡(τ)​‖ϵ−gθτ​(ατ​𝐱+στ​ϵ)‖22],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p^{\text{data}},\,\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),\,\tau}\left[\,w(\tau)\,\big\|\,\bm{\epsilon}-g^{\tau}_{\theta}\!\big(\alpha^{\tau}\mathbf{x}+\sigma^{\tau}\bm{\epsilon}\big)\big\|_{2}^{2}\,\right], (11)

where w⁡(τ)w(\tau) is a time-dependent weighting [59]. The clean-sample, score, and velocity parameterizations are linearly equivalent [59, 103]; we take gθτg^{\tau}_{\theta} as a noise predictor, and the analysis transfers to the other parameterizations.

Generation via Deterministic ODE Updates. At inference time, generation starts from an initial Gaussian noise sample 𝐱T=ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\mathbf{x}^{T}=\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and iteratively maps it to a clean sample by following the reverse probability-flow ODE. The deterministic update used in (3) can be viewed as a first-order Euler step of this ODE, with DDIM [101] and EDM [59] as representative instances. Given the current noisy sample 𝐱τ\mathbf{x}^{\tau}, the predicted clean sample is obtained by inverting the forward path (10):

𝐱^0|τ=𝐱τ−στ​gθτ​(𝐱τ)ατ.\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{0\mid\tau}=\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\tau}-\sigma^{\tau}\,g^{\tau}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau}\right)}{\alpha^{\tau}}. (12)

The sample is then advanced to the next, less-noisy time τ−1\tau-1 by reapplying the forward path to 𝐱^0|τ\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{0\mid\tau}, while using the predicted noise as the noise direction:

𝐱τ−1=ατ−1​𝐱^0|τ+στ−1​gθτ​(𝐱τ).\mathbf{x}^{\tau-1}=\alpha^{\tau-1}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{0\mid\tau}+\sigma^{\tau-1}\,g^{\tau}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau}\right). (13)

Iterating this deterministic update from TT to 00 defines the generative model sampling 𝐱∼fθ\mathbf{x}\sim f_{\theta}. Substituting (12) into (13) recovers the denoising update in (3).

Probability-Flow ODE and Initial-Noise Determinism. In the continuous-time limit, the deterministic updates in (13) correspond to an Euler discretization of the probability-flow ODE associated with the forward path in (10) [103, 59]. This ODE transports samples from the Gaussian prior 𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) to the data distribution pdatap^{\text{data}} along deterministic trajectories. Therefore, the generated sample can be written as ϵ↦fθ​(ϵ)=𝐱0,\bm{\epsilon}\mapsto f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon})=\mathbf{x}^{0}, where fθf_{\theta} denotes the deterministic sampler induced by the trained denoiser. This makes the generated sample a deterministic and differentiable function of the initial noise, justifying the use of ϵ\bm{\epsilon} as a control variable and allowing gradients of downstream criteria to be backpropagated through the sampler.

A.3 Action-conditioned Video World Models

Video world models for robotics have shown promise for policy evaluation and improvement by simulating hard-to-model systems directly from high-dimensional sensor observations [78]. In robotic manipulation, for example, a world model can anticipate how objects may spill, slip, or topple during physical interaction from camera observations [82, 98, 119]. In autonomous driving, it can simulate future scene evolution in complex environments, capturing agent interactions and safety-critical situations directly in image space [38, 50]. These capabilities can support the evaluation and improvement of visuomotor control policies in simulation, reducing reliance on costly, time-consuming, and potentially unsafe real-world trials [78, 125].

Stable Video Diffusion. Recent video world models often build on video generation models [1, 117], which have demonstrated strong ability to synthesize realistic and temporally coherent videos. Rather than learning from scratch, many recent approaches initialize from large-scale video diffusion models and then fine-tune them on domain-specific datasets such as driving or robotic manipulation. A widely used backbone is Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [14], a latent diffusion model for image-to-video generation. SVD uses an encoder–decoder architecture to map RGB frames into a learned latent space, z=ℰ⁡(o)∈ℝ4×H/8×W/8,z=\mathcal{E}(o)\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times H/8\times W/8}, where HH and WW denote the image height and width. The diffusion model is then trained to denoise latent video representations, following an objective of the form in (11), and the generated latents are decoded back into RGB video frames using the decoder.

Action Conditioning. For robotic applications, video world models are conditioned on actions to enable controllable future generation [38, 42]. These actions may correspond to future ego-vehicle controls or trajectories in autonomous driving [38, 50], or to robot action sequences such as end-effector poses, joint-position commands, or low-level control commands in robotic manipulation [42, 65]. In the notation of (11), the denoiser is conditioned on histories and actions, gθτ​(𝐱τ,𝐨hist,𝐚),g^{\tau}_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\tau},\mathbf{o}^{\text{hist}},\mathbf{a}\right), so that the generated future is constrained to be consistent with both the observed history and the specified action sequence. While earlier world models often learned latent dynamics from task-specific observation–action trajectories [43, 46, 48], recent diffusion-based video world models built on SVD typically start from a pretrained video diffusion model and post-train it with action-conditioned data. When trained with conditional dropout, these models can also use classifier-free guidance at sampling time to trade off visual realism and action controllability [53].

History Conditioning. To generate coherent future frames that remain consistent with the conditioning observations, recent video world models incorporate observation history in several ways. Some methods inject conditioning frames by replacing the corresponding noisy latent frames with clean observed latents during sampling [38]; others use progressive or autoregressive sampling with per-frame noise schedules to encourage causal structure across time [17, 50]; and some provide sparse history frames or memory tokens as additional network inputs through attention-based conditioning [42]. These mechanisms help preserve temporal continuity, keep generated futures consistent with the observed history, supporting longer-horizon, autoregressive video generation by conditioning future predictions on previous observations or generated frames.

Application: Policy Evaluation & Improvement. Action-conditioned video world models can support robot learning without repeated real-world rollouts, enabling scalable data generation, planning, policy evaluation, and policy improvement. Because current state-of-the-art video generation models are often slow and memory-intensive, they are typically used offline rather than for real-time planning. Prior work has primarily leveraged action-conditioned video prediction in two ways: (i) using imagined rollouts to evaluate or optimize policies without repeated hardware trials [91, 42, 109, 70, 125], and (ii) generating synthetic trajectories for data augmentation or policy fine-tuning [42, 58, 99, 41, 125]. In particular, recent works report that video world models can serve as simulators for closed-loop evaluation of visuomotor policies, with predicted performance correlating with real-world success rates [42]. Similarly, policies can be improved using video world models, either through reinforcement learning inside imagined rollouts [99] or by searching for successful synthetic trajectories that are then used to fine-tune the policy [41].

While our method can be applied to these broader settings, our experiments focus specifically on the value of steering video world models for robust policy evaluation and improvement. Rather than evaluating a complete robotic policy in a closed loop, we evaluate candidate trajectories that could be produced by a policy and assess their potential failure risks. Similarly, rather than improving policies through closed-loop exploration inside the world model, we use the steered world model to identify failure-prone expert trajectories and reweight them during policy fine-tuning.

A.4 Inference-time Steering of Generative Models

Given a generative model fθf_{\theta} that maps an initial noise sample ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) to a generated sample 𝒙=fθ​(ϵ)\bm{x}=f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon}), inference-time optimization aims to find generations that maximize a user-specified criterion 𝒞\mathcal{C}, while preserving the plausibility of the generated samples with a regularizer Reg⁡(𝒙)\mathrm{Reg}(\bm{x}) that penalizes generations that deviate from the original model distribution. This can be written as

𝒙∗=argmax𝒙𝒞​(𝒙)−α​Reg​(𝒙).\bm{x}^{*}=\argmax_{\bm{x}}\;\mathcal{C}(\bm{x})-\alpha\,\mathrm{Reg}(\bm{x}). (14)

A natural way to realize this objective is to adapt the generative model itself so that it samples from a reward-tilted distribution,

fθ∗​(𝒙)∝fθ​(𝒙)​exp⁡(𝒞⁡(𝒙)α),f_{\theta}^{*}(\bm{x})\propto f_{\theta}(\bm{x})\exp\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{C}(\bm{x})}{\alpha}\right), (15)

which upweights high-criterion samples while remaining close to the original model distribution. However, directly fine-tuning the generator is often impractical for inference-time control: the criterion may change across tasks or users, and fine-tuning requires significant computation for each new criterion. Moreover, preserving closeness to the original distribution can require density estimates that are intractable or prohibitively expensive for high-dimensional generative models [115, 4]. As a result, model adaptation can drift away from the original data distribution and produce implausible generations [33, 54].

Initial Noise Optimization. Initial noise optimization instead keeps the generative model fixed and optimizes only the input noise according to an inference-time criterion evaluated on the generated sample:

ϵ∗=argmaxϵ𝒞​(fθ​(ϵ)).\bm{\epsilon}^{*}=\argmax_{\bm{\epsilon}}\;\mathcal{C}\!\left(f_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon})\right). (16)

This formulation allows arbitrary criteria to be specified at inference time without modifying the model parameters. If the optimized noise remains plausible under the original Gaussian prior, the resulting generation is still induced by the pretrained model distribution, so additional regularization on the generated sample itself is not required.

When 𝒞\mathcal{C} is differentiable, the optimization can be solved by backpropagating through the diffusion sampler [116, 60, 34]. For non-differentiable criteria, prior work estimates gradients of the criterion [106], amortizes the optimization with a hypernetwork [33], or formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem [18, 113]. Since backpropagating through many iterative denoising steps is computationally expensive, several methods further distill diffusion models into one-step generators to make optimization more tractable [34, 84, 33].

A.5 Typical Set of High-Dimensional Gaussian Noise

The typical set describes where samples from a distribution are expected to lie with high probability. It is therefore a notion of probability mass, rather than simply probability density [25, 83]. For a random vector ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈D)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{D}), let p⁡(ϵ)p(\bm{\epsilon}) denote the joint density of the full DD-dimensional Gaussian prior. The δ\delta-typical set can be written as

𝒯δ(D)={ϵ:|−1D​log⁡p⁡(ϵ)−h⁡(𝒩⁡(0,1))|≤δ},\mathcal{T}_{\delta}^{(D)}=\left\{\bm{\epsilon}:\left|-\frac{1}{D}\log p(\bm{\epsilon})-h(\mathcal{N}(0,1))\right|\leq\delta\right\}, (17)

where h⁡(𝒩⁡(0,1))=12​log⁡(2​π​e)h(\mathcal{N}(0,1))=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e) is the differential entropy of a one-dimensional standard Gaussian. The one-dimensional entropy appears because the standard Gaussian prior factorizes across coordinates, p⁡(ϵ)=∏i=1Dp⁡(ϵi)p(\bm{\epsilon})=\prod_{i=1}^{D}p(\epsilon_{i}). Thus, −1D​log⁡p​(ϵ)-\frac{1}{D}\log p(\bm{\epsilon}) is the average information content per coordinate, analogous to the empirical entropy of an i.i.d. sequence. For the isotropic Gaussian prior,

−1D​log⁡p⁡(ϵ)=12​log⁡(2​π)+12​D​‖ϵ‖22.-\frac{1}{D}\log p(\bm{\epsilon})=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2D}\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}. (18)

Therefore, typicality implies ‖ϵ‖22/D≈1\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}/D\approx 1. In high dimensions, Gaussian samples concentrate on a thin shell of radius approximately D\sqrt{D}, rather than near the mode. This illustrates the key distinction between density and typicality: the zero vector has the highest density under the Gaussian prior, but is extremely unlikely to be sampled in high dimensions. Although the Gaussian distribution has full support over ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}, most of its probability mass concentrates on a small subset of that space as DD grows. Equivalently, a typical sample is not characterized only by its likelihood, but by a collection of sample statistics that take values close to their expectations under the Gaussian prior.

Appendix B Inference-time Steering of Video World Models

B.1 Regularizing Noise within the Typical Set of High-Dimensional Gaussian Distribution

In this section, we elaborate on Sec. 4.2, where we impose typical-set constraints during noise optimization. In high-dimensional Gaussian distributions, regions of high probability density do not necessarily coincide with regions of high probability mass, where typical samples concentrate. For example, the zero vector has the highest density under a standard Gaussian, yet it is almost never sampled in high dimensions; instead, typical samples lie on a thin shell with squared norm approximately dd. We refer to this high-mass region as the typical set. As illustrated in Fig. 8, the typical set is distinct from the high-density region, and sampling noise outside the typical set can lead to implausible generations. This distinction is important for diffusion models, which are trained to denoise samples initialized from typical Gaussian noise. If optimization pushes the initial noise toward atypical, low-mass regions of the prior, the denoiser may be evaluated on inputs rarely seen during training, leading to approximation errors and, consequently, implausible or OOD generations.

A common way to encourage typicality is to regularize the norm of the optimized noise, since Gaussian samples exhibit strong norm concentration in high dimensions. Several prior methods have found norm-based regularization sufficient for preserving plausibility in diffusion generation [95, 34, 106]. However, the norm captures only one of the numerous sample statistics of a Gaussian sample. In practice, we find that additional typicality constraints are important for high-dimensional video world models. Thus, as described in Sec. 4.2, we regularize multiple statistics of the optimized noise, including norm concentration, isotropy, and spectral whiteness, each motivated by concentration properties of high-dimensional Gaussian samples.

Fig. 9 illustrates examples of Gaussian noise visualized as 2D images, where each atypical sample violates one statistic of the Gaussian typical set. Violating norm concentration produces noise with globally biased values compared to typical Gaussian noise. Violating isotropy introduces local coordinate patterns that do not appear in typical i.i.d. noise, while violating spectral whiteness produces structured, non-white patterns in the frequency domain.

B.2 Concentration of Gaussian Typical Set Regularizers

Norm Concentration. For Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈D)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{D}), the squared norm satisfies ‖ϵ‖22∼χD2\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{D}, and therefore concentrates sharply around DD. Equivalently, the Euclidean norm, or radius ‖ϵ‖2\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2} concentrates around D\sqrt{D}. Moreover, if R=‖ϵ‖2R=\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}, then RR follows a chi distribution with DD degrees of freedom, whose standard deviation remains bounded independently of DD and approaches 1/21/\sqrt{2} as D→∞D\to\infty. Thus, although the typical radius grows as D\sqrt{D}, the absolute width of the shell containing most Gaussian probability mass remains approximately constant. This motivates penalizing deviations from the typical Gaussian shell in radius:

𝒞norm​(ϵ):=−(‖ϵ‖2−D)2.\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{norm}}(\bm{\epsilon}):=-\left(\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{2}-\sqrt{D}\right)^{2}.
Lemma 1 (Norm concentration of Gaussian noise).

Let ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈D)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{D}). Then, for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1),

ℙ⁡(X−D≥2​D​x+2​x)≤e−x,ℙ⁡(D−X≥2​D​x)≤e−x.\mathbb{P}\!\left(X-D\geq 2\sqrt{Dx}+2x\right)\leq e^{-x},\qquad\mathbb{P}\!\left(D-X\geq 2\sqrt{Dx}\right)\leq e^{-x}.

−2​D​log⁡(2/δ)≤X−D≤2​D​log⁡(2/δ)+2​log⁡(2/δ).-2\sqrt{D\log(2/\delta)}\leq X-D\leq 2\sqrt{D\log(2/\delta)}+2\log(2/\delta).

|XD−1|≤2​log⁡(2/δ)D+2​log⁡(2/δ)D.\left|\frac{X}{D}-1\right|\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{D}}+2\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{D}.

For
